name: Zoe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Neil and I have six thousand free-range laying hens and seventy hectares of wheat and oilseed rape at Elm Tree Farm. My day starts at half six opening the pop-holes, those are the little doors that let the hens out onto the range. Then it's egg collection off the belts, grading, checking the birds for anything off, and the packing station lorry comes Tuesdays and Fridays. Neil does three days a week at the feed mill, so the arable is mostly his on the other days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers, funnily enough. I keep a spreadsheet of lay rates, feed, egg weights, and I can tell you to the penny what a dozen costs us. What wears me out is foxes and bird flu rules. One fox can kill forty birds in a night, and when there's a bird flu order you keep them all shut in for weeks and they hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use the AI thing on the computer now and then, mostly to tidy up letters, and that's about all I'd want from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the spreadsheet, and that's all it ever was. I'd say that at the egg producers' meeting if it came up. I wouldn't post anything, there's enough nonsense online already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means we carry on, and our plan stays the same. Farm till sixty-five, then sell or rent out the land, and Neil and I get a bungalow nearer the girls. Nothing in this picture touches that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now, keep using the AI for letters and the odd sum. We'd keep saving into the farm account at the rate we do, which is about four months of costs. And I'd replace the old egg grader next year, because that's a real problem with real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved that the plan still holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of letters do you use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the packing station cut our price by two pence a dozen and I wanted to argue it without sounding cross. I wrote what I thought, rude bits and all, and asked it to make it polite. It got us one penny back, which over a year is a decent amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the old grader is a real problem. How much would it cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eleven thousand for a good second-hand one. It'd come out of savings, so we'd be down to maybe two months. I'd want two quotes and a look at one working on someone else's farm first.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the spreadsheet, and that's all it ever was. I'd say that at the egg producers' meeting but wouldn't post anything online.
S0.think: It means we carry on and our plan stays the same: farm till sixty-five, then sell or rent out the land and buy a bungalow near our daughters. Nothing in this picture touches that.
S0.do: Carries on as now, using AI for letters and the odd calculation, and keeps saving about four months of costs. Replaces the old egg grader with a second-hand one for about eleven thousand after getting two quotes.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved that the plan still holds.
S0.quote: I wrote what I thought, rude bits and all, and asked it to make it polite. It got us one penny back, which over a year is a decent amount.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe sees everything through her spreadsheet and is proud of knowing her costs to the penny. She already uses AI in a narrow, practical way that pays for itself. Her plan for retirement is clear and the mild scenario leaves it untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds realistic. You can already buy robots that walk round the shed picking up floor eggs and stirring the litter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say each farm should work out what makes sense for them, with real numbers, not hype either way. I'd probably go to the open day at whoever bought a shed robot first and have a good look. That's what I'd tell other people to do as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could be good for us if we're sensible. The shed robots cost less every year, and they'd save my knees. The risk is the big egg firms using it to cut prices, so the savings go to them and not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump. I'd wait a year, watch two or three farms that buy the shed robot, and get their real figures. If it pays back in under five years, I'd buy one, maybe twenty thousand with a grant. And I'd use the AI more for the paperwork side, the bird flu forms and the egg records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried. It's like a new lorry route, you want to see it before you trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which farms would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Fletchers have twelve thousand birds over at Ridgeway, they'll buy first, they always do. And there's a young couple, Sam and Priya, who started three years ago. I'd ask them both for their lay rates before and after, and they'd tell me, we share figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the savings might go to the big egg firms. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much on my own, to be honest. I'd want the producers' group to push for a fair price formula. But I'm not one for marches, I'd rather sit across a table with the numbers.

S1.say: I'd say each farm should work out what makes sense for them with real numbers, not hype either way. I'd go and look at the first local farm to buy a shed robot and tell others to do the same.
S1.think: It could be good for us if we're sensible, because shed robots get cheaper and would save my knees. The risk is the big egg firms using it to cut prices so the savings go to them.
S1.do: Waits a year to watch two or three farms that buy a shed robot and gets their real figures. Buys one for about twenty thousand with a grant if it pays back in under five years, and uses AI more for bird flu forms and egg records.
S1.feel: Uneasy but more interested than worried, wanting to see it before trusting it.
S1.quote: It's like a new lorry route, you want to see it before you trust it.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe's steady style shows clearly: she would wait for proof from neighbours, with a payback rule in mind. Her concern isn't the robots but who keeps the savings. She prefers negotiating with figures to protest, which fits her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. That's quicker than the grader would pay for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, and don't sign anything in the first six months. Lots of people will make bad decisions in a hurry, selling land cheap or buying kit dear. I'd be saying that at the producers' group and to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think egg prices would drop a long way if robot farms can run sheds for almost nothing, and our margin is thin already. We own the land, which helps, but we've got four months of money and a small loan on the shed. Neil's job at the mill might go too, so that's both our incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the grader and stop any spending that doesn't keep the hens alive. In the first year I'd rent the arable land to whichever contractor has the robots, because we couldn't compete on wheat, and keep the hens as long as the numbers worked. I'd also talk to the girls about whether we'd need to bring the bungalow plan forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing sums at the kitchen table at midnight, which Neil hates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sums at midnight look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Egg price on one side, feed and the shed loan on the other, and the gap between them getting smaller every month. I'd colour the cells red when we're losing money. I imagine there'd be quite a lot of red.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't panic in public, but you're doing sums at midnight. Which is the real you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. Not panicking means not doing anything daft, it doesn't mean not worrying. I'd be the calm one at the meeting and the worried one at home, and Neil would see both.

S2.say: I'd say don't panic and don't sign anything in the first six months, because people will sell land cheap or buy kit dear in a hurry. I'd say that at the producers' group and to anyone who asked.
S2.think: Egg prices would fall a long way and our margin is already thin, with four months of money and a small loan on the shed. My husband's job at the feed mill might go too, which is both our incomes.
S2.do: Cancels the grader and stops all spending except what keeps the hens alive. Rents the arable land to a robot contractor within the first year, keeps the hens while the numbers work, and discusses moving retirement plans forward with her daughters.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing sums at the kitchen table at midnight.
S2.quote: I'd colour the cells red when we're losing money. I imagine there'd be quite a lot of red.
S2.fieldNote: Zoe stays practical even in the fast scenario, and renting land to a robot contractor is a calm, sensible move rather than a fight. She is open about the gap between the calm public face and the midnight sums. Her husband's mill job adds a second risk she raised herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's nearly the plan anyway, just squeezed a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the sensible farmers to get ready, and I'd want the producers' group to help people work out their own figures. I'd say it plainly and without fuss. No point frightening people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be all right if we plan it well. We'd buy the shed robot once it's proven, maybe year two, run the hens a few more years with less work, and sell or rent out at sixty-three instead of sixty-five. My knees would thank me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd pay off the shed loan early instead of buying the grader. I'd get the Fletchers' and Sam and Priya's robot figures and decide by the end of year two. And I'd sit down with an adviser about renting out the land at sixty-three, so we know what it's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. I'd have a plan, and a plan on paper calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the girls about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the plan in one sentence and send them the spreadsheet if they wanted. Amy would want it, she's a maths teacher. Beth would say, Mum, just tell me you're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change anything for Neil?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell him to think about the mill now. He's sixty, he could stop when the robots come and help me with the hens till we sell. That would actually be quite nice, the two of us on the farm together for a couple of years.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for sensible farmers to get ready, and I'd want the producers' group to help people work out their own figures. I'd say it plainly, with no point frightening people.
S3.think: We'd be all right if we plan well: buy the shed robot once proven, run the hens with less work and sell or rent out at sixty-three. My knees would thank me.
S3.do: Pays off the shed loan early instead of buying the grader and decides on a shed robot by the end of year two using neighbours' figures. Sees an adviser about renting out the land at sixty-three.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in control, calmed by having a plan on paper.
S3.quote: I'd tell them the plan in one sentence and send them the spreadsheet if they wanted.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year picture fits neatly into Zoe's existing plan and she simply brings it forward two years. She'd still wait for proof before buying a robot. The idea of working the farm with her husband before selling came out warmly and seemed new to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then that one's mostly for whoever buys the farm from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should use it, but not in a rush. Buy what's proven, retrain if your job's going, and don't believe anyone who says they know exactly how it'll go. I'd say that at the group and probably at the pub quiz too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change our plan at all. We'd sell at sixty-five, a few years before it arrives, and the buyer would have to deal with it. The worry is that the farm might sell for less if buyers think robots make it worth less, or more, I genuinely don't know which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the plan, buy the shed robot when the price drops, maybe year four or five, and keep saving. I'd get the farm valued every couple of years to watch which way the price is going. And I'd keep using AI for the letters, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about the land price, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know if the land would be worth more or less. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It's most of our pension, that land. But I can't control it, so I'd rather watch the numbers than lie awake about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young couple, Sam and Priya. They've got twenty-five years of farming ahead of them and a big loan. I'd tell them to get good at the robots, because they'll be running them for most of their working lives.

S4.say: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should use it, but not in a rush: buy what's proven and retrain if your job's going. I'd also say not to believe anyone who claims to know exactly how it'll go.
S4.think: It doesn't change our plan, because we'd sell at sixty-five before it arrives. I don't know if robots would make the farm sell for more or less, and the land is most of our pension.
S4.do: Carries on with the plan and buys the shed robot when prices drop, around year four or five, while keeping up savings. Gets the farm valued every couple of years and uses AI a bit more for letters.
S4.feel: Calm, and curious about what will happen to the land price.
S4.quote: It's most of our pension, that land. But I can't control it, so I'd rather watch the numbers than lie awake about them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zoe's plan holds and she sells before the change arrives. The only open question is the land price, and she answered it with numbers rather than worry. Her concern goes to the young couple nearby with a long career and a big loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd lose both incomes at once and the egg price would fall before we could do anything. What would help is a fair price formula for eggs, so the packing stations can't take all the savings, and some kind of help for farmers who are close to retiring to wind down properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. A robot can pick up eggs, fine, but the hens notice who walks through the shed. When I'm off sick and Neil does it, the lay rate drops a bit, I've got it in the spreadsheet.

headlineQuote: When I'm off sick and Neil does it, the lay rate drops a bit, I've got it in the spreadsheet.
portrait: Zoe Abbott is a 58-year-old who runs six thousand free-range hens and seventy hectares of wheat and oilseed rape with her husband Neil, who also works at a feed mill. She keeps a spreadsheet of everything, uses AI now and then to polish letters, and won't buy any machine until she's seen the real figures from neighbours. She's calm in the mild scenarios and uneasy in the steady one, where she'd wait a year then buy a shed robot if it paid back. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because both household incomes and the egg price would fall at once, while five or ten years simply fit into her plan to sell and retire.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because she and her husband would lose both incomes at once and the egg price would fall before they could act.
whatWouldHelp: A fair price formula for eggs so packing stations can't take all the savings, and help for farmers near retirement to wind down properly.
